#42814. Intel faced a choice: Give Trump 10% or face the consequences

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1925 w)
📖 Baca
Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Intel faced a choice: Give Trump 10% or face the consequences

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1925 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the message from the Trump administration to one of the world’s leading semiconductor companies was clear: Give the US government a chunk of your company.
  • Do not make the “mistake of thinking that this is a negotiation,” Commerce Department lawyer David Shapiro told the chief financial officer of the Intel Corporation in August 2025, according to internal notes from a company call contained in a federal lawsuit.
  • Recent findings suggest that shapiro acknowledged that “the Board could choose not to accept the offer,” according to a summary of his remarks prepared for Intel’s directors.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the message from the Trump administration to one of the world’s leading semiconductor companies was clear: Give the US government a chunk of your company. Right now. Or else.

Do not make the “mistake of thinking that this is a negotiation,” Commerce Department lawyer David Shapiro told the chief financial officer of the Intel Corporation in August 2025, according to internal notes from a company call contained in a federal lawsuit. “The President is expecting to announce a deal on these terms on Friday.”.

Recent findings suggest that shapiro acknowledged that “the Board could choose not to accept the offer,” according to a summary of his remarks prepared for Intel’s directors. But the Trump administration official “noted that rejection will have consequences that [Shapiro] cannot predict.”.

Recent findings suggest that days later, the board gave the administration what it wanted. “It is my Great Honor to report that the United States of America now fully owns and controls 10% of INTEL,” Donald Trump posted to his social platform. “The United States paid nothing for these Shares, and the Shares are now valued at approximately $11 Billion Dollars. This is a great Deal for America.”.

President Trump was similarly jubilant on Monday, announcing that he had “convinced” Nvidia’s board of directors to rehire chief executive Jensen Huang. The proclamation was a shock. But it wasn’t entirely without precedent.

Fifteen months earlier, the Trump administration had interfered with the leadership decisions at another major chipmaker, court documents allege. Then, as now, allegations swirled that the company’s CEO was too close to China. Then, as now, the Trump administration dealt itself into the company’s financial future.

According to recent reports, it’s part of a broader shift within the government in general and the Commerce Department in particular, a former member of that department tells WIRED. Out are old metrics “like creating jobs or the US being more competitive or owning more of the market share,” this ex-Trump administration official says. When dealing with private companies, a single overriding concern is: “Are you going to give back to the government in cash?”.

Documents unredacted as part of a shareholder’s lawsuit against Intel’s board show how far the administration has been willing to go to get what it wants. The lawsuit’s allegations were previously reported by WP Intelligence.

“The Board, operating under the shadow of the President’s threats,” the lawsuit alleges, “caved to the government’s extortion.” A second case, asking for internal records, was filed in April by the same shareholder, Richard Paisner, against Nvidia.

“It’s just straight-up coercion,” says Scott Lincicome, a vice president at the libertarian Cato Institute. “The tech giant starts making decisions not based on what’s best for the company in the short or long term, what’s best for shareholders, but what’s best for politics and what the government is demanding.”.

According to recent reports, “That’s not what you want from any company,” he adds. “When you’re talking about the world’s most innovative companies and these kinds of bleeding-edge technologies that have not only huge economic implications but national security ones, then that’s a huge problem.”.

In a recent development, representatives for Intel declined to comment for this story. The White House, Commerce Department, and Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment.

Recent findings suggest that the parallels between Nvidia’s government-assisted autogolpe and Intel’s alleged forced sale aren’t exact. In the Intel case, Trump all but accused the company’s boss of being compromised by Beijing; in the Nvidia situation, the president reportedly dismissed concerns from his own intelligence agencies about the executive’s connections to China. But both instances show a growing fusion of private enterprise and public office.

During the Biden administration, Intel won awards for up to $11 billion in government grants and contracts, much of it under the CHIPS Act, which was meant to help build semiconductor manufacturing and assembly plants in America and bolster domestic research.

At the time, there was some grumbling inside the Commerce Department, which administered the CHIPS and Science Act grants, about funding what was seen as a “failing incumbent” in the semiconductor space, says the former official. (Intel had, in recent years, fallen on hard times.) But by March 2025, Intel had received about $2.2 billion of the grants. That’s when President Trump told Congress that the CHIPS Act was “a horrible, horrible thing.” The rest of Intel’s money was put on hold, tied to hitting certain milestones, while the administration remarked it was renegotiating the deals.

Sources indicate that the same month Lip-Bu Tan was hired as Intel’s fresh CEO. Soon after, his ties to China made him a Trump target, when Reuters reported that Tan had invested in “hundreds of Chinese tech firms,” some with connections to Beijing’s military. Tan’s former firm, Cadence Design Systems, pleaded guilty to violating US sanctions by selling semiconductor designs to a restricted Chinese military university, and agreed to pay more than $140 million in fines. Tan was never personally charged, but the violations happened while he was the CEO.

Two weeks later, the president was watching Maria Bartiromo’s show on the Fox Business Network. It mentioned a letter a senator had sent Intel about the China ties. Trump posted, “The CEO of INTEL is highly CONFLICTED and must resign, immediately. There is no other solution to this problem.”.

Industry observers note that tan went to the Oval Office on August 11 to see if there was, in fact, another solution. He got 40 minutes with the president, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.

It has been revealed that tan claimed his experience in China was a strength, not a detriment. According to the book Regime Change, Tan argued that there was no way he could’ve known about every one of the deals his many companies made; Trump, who had his own sprawling business empire, surely knew what that was like. Tan promised to give up his holdings in China, according to a letter Tan shared with Intel’s board, and put any proceeds into a blind trust.

Recent findings suggest that “The primary goal was to eliminate any worries about Lip-Bu himself, his Cadence background, and his investments with China,” according to a source with knowledge of the matter. But there were major financial concerns for Intel, too. “We had declining revenues and needed money.”.

Neither Tan’s letter, excerpted in the complaint, nor Trump’s social media posts praising the CEO after the meeting mentioned anything about giving the government a chunk of the tech giant. Yet Trump later insisted that a deal had been cooked up right then and there. “He came in, he saw me, we talked for a while. I liked him a lot, I thought he was very good,” the president told The Wall Street Journal. “I remarked, ‘You know what? I think the United States should be given 10% of Intel.’ And he said, ‘I would consider that.’”.

“I should’ve asked for more. It was so easy,” Trump later recalled.

Recent findings suggest that according to the court filing’s review of Intel’s internal documents, Shapiro—a former partner at the New York law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz—made a verbal offer on August 18. Ultimately, in exchange for the cut of Intel, the Trump administration would free up the $8.9 billion US government grants that it had already won. They wanted about a tenth of the firm’s stock for free, in exchange for Washington keeping the commitment it had already made.

Industry observers note that then came the call in which Shapiro insisted there was no room for negotiation. “The board needs to consider,” he noted, according to Intel’s summary of his remarks included in the court documents, the “benefits of having a friend in this administration and what the administration can do to help Intel (including with customers).”.

Sources indicate that intel’s board met, and decided they hated the deal. “The economic terms that had been proposed [by] the Administration were not, in their current form, attractive to the company,” minutes of the meeting, reprinted in the lawsuit, noted.

Sources indicate that but they went ahead with it anyway. Paisner’s lawyers say in the court documents the board took the offer thrust forward by the administration. Intel’s attorneys disagree, arguing in their motion to dismiss that there was some back-and-forth deal-making, and it made the agreement more favorable to the organization. The grants became “immediately available” while “strategically aligning the interests of Intel’s stockholders and the US Government.”.

It has been revealed that on August 25, Lutnick released a video with Tan, sitting side-by-side on cushioned chairs. “I really look forward to have the US government be my shareholder,” Tan turned to Lutnick and mentioned. “And we can work together and make Intel great again.”.

Inside the firm, the video was “a surprise to everyone,” according to a source with direct knowledge of the matter. Some employees joked that it was reminiscent of a “hostage video.”.

Not long after that, Nvidia—led by Tan’s friend Jensen Huang—made a $5 billion investment in Intel. “I love seeing their stock price go up, making the USA RICHER, AND RICHER,” Trump posted. “Who would not want to make deals like that?”.

In a recent development, deals, plural. On the day Tan was hauled to the Oval Office, Trump announced that his administration had been negotiating separately with Huang. The Nvidia leader was beyond eager to sell more of his semiconductors to China. “And I remarked, if I’m going to do that, I want you to pay us as a country something,’” Trump said. They settled on 15 percent of all sales of the H20 model chip. Months after that, they cut a second deal: a 25 percent bounty on sales of Nvidia’s even-more advanced H200 chips.

In their lawsuit against Nvidia, Paisner’s attorneys argue the surcharges amount to “unlawful taxes,” and that the board’s “decisions to enter into such agreements are the product of mismanagement and breaches of fiduciary duty.”.

In court, NVIDIA’s lawyers insisted that the company “did not enter into any illegal ‘agreement’ with the government but instead engaged with the government and stated that it would comply with federal regulations.” Moreover, the attorneys say Paisner is trying to make a political point, rather than a legal one. “When asked about his purpose in bringing this action,” they write, “Paisner was candid: ‘It’s to make a public point of how NVIDIA conducts itself.’”.

In a recent development, the attorneys wrote this in May, months before Nvidia’s and Huang’s recent drama. Last week, board chair Harvey Jones stated on the tech giant’s quarterly earnings call that it did “not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” citing his “disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms.” (Not to mention mounting evidence that the company’s most sophisticated chips were making their way to China, in violation of US law.) But, according to The Fresh York Times, after days of pressure from top administration officials, the company and the government essentially struck a deal Sunday night to reinstate Huang.

In a recent development, “Don’t think for a second that politics ever play a role in this tech giant, not even a little bit,” Huang said during his first company-wide meeting after rejoining the company, WIRED reported. “We are the most apolitical company. I don’t love that we talk about politics here. Take it home. I love that we talk about work here.”.

Additional reporting by Lauren Goode.

These instances are powered by AWS Graviton5 processors, the fifth generation of custom-designed CPUs, which deliver the best price performance for a broad range of workloads running on Amazon EC2.

Recent findings suggest that M9gd instances deliver up to 25% better compute performance than AWS Graviton4-based M8gd instances. They are up to 30% faster for databases, up to 35% faster for web applications, and up to 35% faster for machine learning. These instances are built on the sixth-generation AWS Nitro System and are the first to feature the Nitro Isolation Engine. The Isolation Engine uses formal verification to provide mathematical assurance that customer workloads are isolated from each other and from AWS operators, pioneering a new standard for mathematically proven cloud security.

Sources indicate that M9gd instances serve a broad range of general-purpose workloads, including application servers, microservices, gaming, caching, and containers. They also deliver the performance needed for agentic AI use cases like real-time reasoning, code generation, and multi-step orchestration. M9gd instances also offer local NVMe-based SSD block-level storage for workloads that need high-speed, low-latency local storage for scratch space, temporary files, and caches.

Sources indicate that M9gd instances are available for purchase in this region via Savings Plans, On-Demand, Spot Instances, Dedicated Instances, or Dedicated Hosts. Level up your compute with AWS Graviton and get started with M9gd today.

#42810. Here’s Everything You Can Do With With the Latest Gemini AI on Android Auto

Here’s Everything You Can Do With With the Latest Gemini AI on Android Auto

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (907 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google Assistant is being replaced by Google’s more advanced Gemini AI across all platforms, and that includes Android Auto.
  • You’ll see a message onscreen announcing the arrival of Gemini, with the latest “spark” icon (a small star by a sound-wave-like icon), instead of the traditional microphone when the AI is active.
  • If you've used Gemini before on your phone, on the web, or somewhere else, then you're going to know the extras that it brings over Google Assistant.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google Assistant is being replaced by Google’s more advanced Gemini AI across all platforms, and that includes Android Auto. If the switch hasn’t happened yet on your own vehicle’s dashboard, then it should happen soon.

You’ll see a message onscreen announcing the arrival of Gemini, with the latest “spark” icon (a small star by a sound-wave-like icon), instead of the traditional microphone when the AI is active.

If you've used Gemini before on your phone, on the web, or somewhere else, then you're going to know the extras that it brings over Google Assistant. It's a truly natural conversation partner that can dig deep into information available online, and respond to a much wider range of queries. Here's what the upgraded app can do specifically when you're traveling on the road.

All of the standard commands you might have already been using are still here, of course, like "navigate home" or “Where's the nearest Walmart?” With Gemini though, there's much more flexibility in what you can say without the AI getting confused or misunderstanding what you're asking about.

Sources indicate that for example, your questions can be multilayered. Something like "find the nearest coffee shop that has a drive-thru and is open now" will look for those exact criteria. You're also able to ask context-sensitive follow-up questions, such as "What time will it shut?" or "How long will it take to get there?" if you need further details.

You can ask more general questions too, such as "tell me more about the place I'm heading to" or "Is there outdoor seating?” But bear in mind that Gemini will be limited to scouring the data on Google Maps for its information. (It's a disembodied AI that's never been anywhere.) If it doesn't know the answer to something, it should tell you that.

Overall, it's smarter in every aspect. I was recently navigating a difficult junction and couldn't work out whether the map was sending me left or right. I asked Gemini, "Will I be traveling east or west after the next turn?" and it figured out the answer. That helped me avoid veering off in the wrong direction.

One of the major benefits of having a voice-controlled AI in the car is having it handle messaging and audio tasks without you needing to take your eyes off the road or fish around for a button. If you tell Gemini to “read my last message,” it'll speak it out for you and give you the opportunity to reply. You can also specify the app, otherwise Google Messages will be used by default—Google Chat and WhatsApp are among the others that are supported.

In a recent development, gemini is able to give you summaries of group chats, which is really handy when you're on a drive and the conversations you're involved in are building up message after message that you can't check. Name a group chat in a supported app and ask for a summary, or just request summaries of unread messages. You'll be able to get the gist without checking each individual message.

Recent findings suggest that the usual array of audio commands are here, carried over from Google Assistant, so you can quickly start or stop audio in your music, podcast, radio, and audiobook apps. As well as continuing from where you left off, you can also name artists, albums, and playlists that you want to queue up. YouTube Music and Spotify are among the apps supported, if you need to specify one.

In a recent development, another extra from Gemini is being able to ask about the artist or song that's at the moment playing, and get more information on it. You might want to learn the history of a particular band, find out how long a certain song was at number one, or even get recommendations based on what's currently playing—just ask Gemini.

In a recent development, much more than Google Assistant, Gemini can help you learn something or develop some ideas while you're behind the wheel. If you're on the way to a movie premiere, you can ask Gemini about the history of the film, the director, and the actors, and it'll remember the context of your conversation. (It'll all get synced back to the Gemini app on your other devices.).

Sources indicate that voice commands such as “help me prepare for my interview” or “come up with ideas for a quick and easy meal to make for dinner" will initiate a chat with Gemini that you can continue throughout your journey—and hopefully arrive well-prepared or with dinner sorted (or whatever it is). Maybe don’t ask about anything too mind-bending, as you’ll still need to concentrate on driving.

Sources indicate that gemini will ask along the way for any information it needs about what you’re interviewing for or the ingredients you’ve got at home. You can also ask Gemini to quiz you on a certain topic or run a query on something you see on the journey—like a landmark or a restaurant you go past.

Recent findings suggest that finally, there’s always the weather: Gemini will give you forecasts for the areas and specific locations you give it, on whatever day you want within the next week or so. Perhaps more useful for journeys are questions like “When is the rain going to stop?” or “What are the weather conditions like at my destination?” which will help you plan your trip.

Sources indicate that amazon CloudWatch Omni alerts can now automatically create PagerDuty incidents, so notifications flow directly into your existing incident management workflows. This reduces mean time to resolution (MTTR) by eliminating manual notification steps and ensuring consistent incident workflows.

It has been revealed that cloudWatch Omni is a fully managed AI-powered observability experience built on open standards that unifies monitoring for AI agents, applications, and infrastructure. PagerDuty is an incident management platform that routes alerts to the right on-call responders and coordinates their response. When an Omni alert fires, Omni creates a PagerDuty incident. In PagerDuty, Omni alerts follow your existing on-call schedules and escalation policies, so critical alerts reach the right responder wherever they are, at any hour. Omni alerts include severity, the affected service, and a link back to the related data in Omni, so responders have the context they need to diagnose the problem.

For PagerDuty integration in Amazon CloudWatch Omni regional availability, see Supported Regions for CloudWatch Omni.

To learn more, visit Amazon CloudWatch Omni documentation and refer to the Omni PagerDuty integration page.

When IT slows down, everyone feels it: employees are blocked waiting on support, onboarding is painful, rolling out new tools gets bottlenecked, and entire company initiatives end up stalled.

Yet despite ITâs central role, the last decade of tooling has not truly empowered them. The powerful tools are heavy to set up and brittle to maintain; the easy-to-use tools focus on narrow use cases and deflection rather than true automation. IT teams are eager to automate and are more technical than business users. They have experimented with scripts, workflow builders, and more, but the limitations of all these tools still force them to spend the majority of their time on manual work, preventing them from focusing on higher-impact work and enabling the rest of their organizations.

Recent findings suggest that jake and Alex, the co-founders of Serval, experienced this firsthand at Verkada, where they led Product and Engineering and sold primarily to IT teams. They heard the same half-joking request countless times, and it wasnât about Verkadaâs products. They would ask customers, âWhat else can we build for you?â and IT leaders would reply, âCan you fix my helpdesk too?â These conversations led them to two key insights:.

The first was that true automation only works if it is faster to automate something forever than to do it manually once.

The second came from watching the few IT leaders who did take the time to build automations. They would first describe the workflow in one simple sentence, then reveal a sprawling tree of branches, nodes, conditions, and edge cases. Jake and Alex wondered: what if you could actually build the entire automation the same way you describe it? What if one simple sentence truly was enough?

These insights were not possible to execute on in the past. Prior generations of AI were not strong enough to make it work, which meant IT teams continued working through manual tasks. That has now changed. With modern LLMs, code generation, and reasoning capabilities, it is finally possible to build a platform where âautomate foreverâ is faster than âfix once.â.

Serval is built precisely to deliver on this, and the team is not stopping there. They are using this moment not only to build a system of automation, but to rethink the entire ITSM system of record. As our own Sequoia IT leader, Leon, shared when they chose to become a Serval customer: âServal is not AI for ITSM â it is ITSM built from AI.â.

At the heart of the platform is an AI automation engine that lets teams go from a simple sentence to a deployment-ready automation. IT can describe workflows in natural language, then refine them further â either in natural language or all the way down to code when needed. This combination of being simple enough for anyone to use, yet deep enough for the most advanced IT builders, has resonated strongly with customers. The workflows are fully explainable and traceable, with all necessary permissions included, giving IT teams complete visibility and control and eliminating hallucination risk.

While their automation engine integrates with existing systems of records, Serval has also built a full-fledged ITSM platform, including a ticketing system, an access management product, an asset management solution, and more. Serval is both the system of engagement and the system of record. This gives IT a single place to build and orchestrate automations, enforce security and compliance, and capture the data that compounds their automation over time.

Recent findings suggest that customer feedback has been exceptional. We consistently heard how easy Serval is to use, yet how powerful, traceable, and trustworthy its automations are in practice. IT leaders described day-to-day operations being transformed â automation percentages rising every week, employee satisfaction increasing, and IT teams finally having the bandwidth to tackle projects that had been stuck on the back burner for years.

What was also exceptional, and, to be perfectly honest, not something we expected to hear at this stage:.

Sources indicate that automation swiftly spread beyond IT into HR, Finance, Legal, Engineering, Security, and more. In some cases, companies have churned off dedicated software vendors for some departments because they rebuilt their workflows directly in Serval.

At Sequoia, the last time we heard such customer feedback that supports the thesis of IT system of record empowering horizontal enterprise automation was 16 years ago, when we partnered with ServiceNow. That is why we were so eager to partner with Serval and preempt their Series B round.

AWS Lambda now supports orchestrating MicroVMs with Lambda durable functions

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (319 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that today, AWS introduces a developer preview of a new extension for orchestrating Lambda MicroVMs with Lambda durable functions.
  • With Lambda durable functions, you can build resilient, multi-step applications and AI workflows that run for up to one year, with built-in checkpointing and automatic retries.
  • In a recent development, the MicroVM extension is available as a developer preview for the AWS Durable Execution SDK for TypeScript and Python.

It has been revealed that today, AWS introduces a developer preview of a new extension for orchestrating Lambda MicroVMs with Lambda durable functions. The extension adds durable operations for running work on MicroVMs and managing their lifecycle. You can use the new operations to build software factories, security scanners, or orchestrate CI/CD jobs that run untrusted or agent-generated code in isolated sandboxes.

With Lambda durable functions, you can build resilient, multi-step applications and AI workflows that run for up to one year, with built-in checkpointing and automatic retries. Lambda MicroVMs are a serverless compute primitive that provides VM-level isolation, near-instant launch and resume, and state preservation for running user-generated or AI-generated code. With this launch, you can run individual tasks in a MicroVM or launch a MicroVM session, where tasks share the same files and memory. The durable function manages the MicroVM lifecycle and runs each task as a durable operation. It checkpoints progress, retries failed tasks, and refreshes MicroVM tokens as needed. A single durable function can orchestrate multiple MicroVMs in parallel, and you can trigger it from event sources such as Amazon SQS or Amazon EventBridge. An optional worker library runs inside your MicroVM image to receive tasks, send heartbeats, and report results.

In a recent development, the MicroVM extension is available as a developer preview for the AWS Durable Execution SDK for TypeScript and Python. To get started, add the extensions package to your function alongside the Durable Execution SDK (JS/TS, Python) and add the MicroVM worker library (JS/TS, Python) to your MicroVM image. Developer preview features may change, so do not use them for production workloads. The extension is available in all AWS Regions that support Lambda durable functions and Lambda MicroVMs.

To learn more, see the MicroVM orchestration documentation and the sample application. To share feedback, open an concern in the Durable Execution SDK GitHub repository in JavaScript or Python.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the best MagSafe wallets are compact, slim, and svelte, and they attach securely to your iPhone (or MagSafe-compatible case). They are handy if you only want to carry a few cards, like your work badge or train fare. MagSafe wallets are also great for anyone who wants to travel light and forgo a traditional wallet entirely. We’ve tested dozens, and our favorites are below.

Read our MagSafe guides for more useful accessory recommendations, including the Best MagSafe Accessories, Best MagSafe Power Banks, Best MagSafe Wireless Chargers, and Best MagSafe Grips.

Updated November 2026: I’ve added new wallets to our honorable mentions section and removed discontinued products. I’ve also checked for accuracy throughout.

In a recent development, magSafe is Apple’s magnetic technology built into the iPhone 12, iPhone 13, iPhone 14, iPhone 15, iPhone 16 (excluding the iPhone 16e), iPhone 17, iPhone 18 Pro, and iPhone Duo. It features a hidden ring of magnets on the back of the phone and was developed to create a faster, more precise wireless charging system. Those magnets also connect to accessories such as external batteries, car mounts, and wallets.

According to recent reports, if you use a case on your iPhone, make sure it’s also MagSafe (the case will have a ring of magnets inside). This will ensure a proper connection with MagSafe accessories. If you use a non-MagSafe case, the connection will be very weak, and MagSafe products may just slide off your iPhone. We have lots of case recommendations in our guides:.

When buying a wallet, make sure it supports MagSafe or Qi2 connections. The product description should indicate this prominently. Qi2 is the wireless charging standard, and all MagSafe iPhones support Qi2. Android phones now also support Qi2, and some have magnets inside, like the Google Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 series (Google calls it Pixelsnap).

MagSafe wallets use the same ring of magnets that lets them snap directly onto the back of the iPhone or a MagSafe- or supported Qi2 case. This gives the wallet a strong and secure hold on your device. The wallets we’ve included in this guide all have the MagSafe seal of approval.

Apple first introduced MagSafe for its iPhones in 2020. The following models support the technology:.

Do MagSafe Wallets Work With Android Phones?

Recent findings suggest that to use a MagSafe wallet with an Android phone (or the iPhone 16e), you’ll need to use a MagSafe case. Several case manufacturers have started adding a ring of magnets to Android phone cases to bring the same magnetic experience native to iPhones.

Will a MagSafe Wallet Demagnetize My Credit Card?

No, MagSafe will not demagnetize your credit cards. Credit cards have magnetic stripe encoding strong enough to resist demagnetization, and the MagSafe wallets in this guide include a built-in shield designed to keep your cards safe. However, you may run into complications with hotel key cards and some gift cards. Keep those away as a precaution.

It has been revealed that I use a MagSafe wallet every day as my primary wallet. I check that it snaps firmly onto the iPhone or MagSafe case—and that it doesn’t slide off when I take my phone out of my pocket, bag, or jacket. I also make sure cards fit well in the sleeve and don’t fall out. I only recommend wallets that feel durable, are easy to use, and can hold the standard amount of cards (at least two to three). I occasionally call on my fellow WIRED reviewers for long-term testing or to check out newly introduced models.

UAG’s Metropolis MagSafe wallet is on the spendier side, but you won’t be replacing it in a year or two. It is lightweight yet robust with Kevlar construction. There’s a large slot on the back that can hold up to three cards, and you can unfold the wallet and store an additional three (or cash) inside. It also pulls double duty as a stand if you need to prop up your phone, and you can orient your phone in landscape or portrait mode. —Molly Higgins.

Smartish’s MagSafe wallet makes me wish all wallets had a slot on the side to push out the cards. I never had to take it off my phone to access cards. Just give the spacious side opening a little push with your thumb, and the cards slide out. My cards remained secure, and I never had an issue with them falling out. It’s made of vegan leather, and Smartish offers a few fun designs. —Brenda Stolyar.

This luxe, super-thin leather MagSafe wallet from Nomad has Apple’s Find My feature built in, so you can easily locate it in the Find My app if it’s misplaced. That does mean you need to charge the wallet, but don’t worry, there's no proprietary cable here. Instead, the wallet can be wirelessly charged on any MagSafe or Qi2 charger; once it’s fully charged, the battery lasts for five months. Easy peasy.

It’s made from vegetable-tanned Horween leather with a polycarbonate frame, and it can hold up to four cards. (A less expensive version that uses Nomad's Camino leather is also available.) It looks classy, and it’s great for anyone with a tendency to lose things. —Molly Higgins.

Note that Nomad also sells a dedicated tracker card, which can add Find My to any wallet but will take up valuable space in a MagSafe version.

I love this wallet from Moft, which is compatible with Apple Find My, so you always know where it is. It’s relatively standard-looking, but it has a built-in tripod, which came in handy numerous times when I wanted to film a quick outfit check or take a group photo. It raises your phone camera to 8 inches high, and the wallet is very sturdy, so you can dial in the right angle. It works in landscape or portrait orientation. With space for two cards, it isn’t the roomiest but is rich in features. —Louryn Strampe.

Industry observers note that you can always rely on Casetify for unique designs. Its Snappy MagSafe wallet is available in various styles and colors. It’s slim, durable, and sleek—the illustrations haven’t faded after months of use. It’s made from vegan leather (aka plastic), but Casetify uses BioVeg, derived from recycled polyester and vegetable oil from non-food and GMO-free corn crops.

It has been revealed that it can hold up to three cards, and there’s a built-in shield that protects them from magnetic damage. My only gripe is that it can be a little difficult to pull the cards out when the wallet is attached to your phone or case. I typically have to detach it and use the opening from the back to slide out the cards. —Brenda Stolyar.

Recent findings suggest that ridge’s metal MagSafe wallet feels solid and high-quality. A few of us tested it, and it reliably held our setups, including one tester’s daily carry of eight cards plus a thicker tracking card. The magnets could be stronger, but Ridge does sell a strengthening tray that might be useful if you’re concerned.

According to recent reports, this wallet can be a little weird to use at first, but you build up muscle memory quickly. There’s a finger slot for pushing cards out, and you slide them back in on the opposite side. Ridge also includes a Torx screwdriver and extra screws, which are useful for switching out the plates, adding or subtracting room for cards, or adding on accessories like the brand’s wallet chain or cash strap. —Louryn Strampe.

Most MagSafe wallets are designed to hold just a few cards, but I love the Moft Snap Field because it can hold so much more. You get plenty of storage space for cards—technically up to eight cards, though more reasonably seven—alongside a dedicated slot for an extra SIM card and a SIM card ejector.

It has been revealed that that extra room already puts the Snap Field a step ahead of most other MagSafe wallets, but you can also store just about anything you want inside. It uses a folding design held together by magnets, so you can quickly throw in cash, coins, or paper cards. Regardless of what you store inside, you can easily get to your cards with a pull tab. And, if all of that wasn’t enough, the backing that attaches to your phone can pop out and function as a kickstand. —Jacob Roach.

It has been revealed that ESR’s MagSafe wallet isn’t bulky, but it also isn’t so thin that it feels insubstantial. It doubles as a kickstand and sticks to my phone reliably. There’s space for five cards—three in the external pockets, plus another two on the inside. I really like the clear window that keeps my ID separate and handy to flash when I get carded. This wallet is simple, but that’s the beauty of it, and it’s affordable to boot. If you want something basic, it’s a good option to consider. Just keep in mind that the included RFID-blocking card probably isn’t necessary. —Louryn Strampe.

Industry observers note that casely’s wallet is made of hard silicone, so it’s slightly heavier and thicker than the other ones I’ve tested. It feels similar to having a MagSafe battery pack on the back. I don’t mind the extra weight and thickness because it makes it easier to grip my phone case. There’s a dedicated slot at the bottom that makes sliding cards out a breeze. Just know that if you pair it with the complementary Casely case, the whole thing is bulky. But darn if it doesn’t look cute. —Brenda Stolyar.

Sources indicate that I’m obsessed with PopSockets grips—I have one on my phone and one on my Kindle. If you’re also a fan and don’t want to get rid of the accessory with a MagSafe wallet, well, you don’t have to. The Popwallet+ is both a PopSockets grip and a wallet. It fits up to three cards (or more, depending on the thickness), and the cloth opening at the bottom makes it easy to push out the cards. The grip works the same way a standard one does, with the ability to expand and collapse. You can swap out the tops if you ever get bored with the design. —Brenda Stolyar.

Supcase’s MagFlip wallet and stand is extremely sturdy, and feels unbreakable. It’s constructed almost entirely out of metal, fitted with huge magnets that never let go and thick hinges around the body. You can store up to five cards in the wallet itself, and there’s an RFID-blocking card that sits at the end, though this kind of protection is largely unnecessary.

It has been revealed that it doubles as a two-height stand as well. You can kick the wallet back and prop your phone up, but if you rotate the wallet around, you can position your phone even higher with a kickstand that keeps everything stable. Even with the rugged, almost militarized construction, SupCase still offers a handful of attractive colors, including one that combines a faux leather exterior with regal gold accents. —Jacob Roach.

A lot of MagSafe wallets just feel like a pocket on the back of your phone. This one from ESR feels like an actual wallet. It comes in a variety of stylish options with a slick metal-tipped clasp and detailed construction. There’s a clear window for your ID, a roomy card pocket, and a compartment that can hold two bills. The card compartment can technically hold up to four cards, but I prefer two or three for easier access. If you want space for cash as well as the other essentials, or you want a leather-type wallet that has more design choices than some competitors, I recommend this one. —Louryn Strampe.

Looks like you need some MagSafe for your MagSafe. Look no further than the Valentinus wallet from Spigen. It’s constructed out of polyurethane leather and can technically hold three cards (I’m able to easily fit four). It comes with a handy card cutout at the bottom so you can quickly thumb through them. The real draw is an extra MagSafe ring built into the back of the wallet.

Stack a MagSafe grip on the back, mount your phone to a MagSafe car stand, or attach whatever other MagSafe accessory you want; you don’t need to take off your wallet first. You can’t charge your phone through it, but the convenience of using other accessories while keeping your wallet attached is worth the price of admission. —Jacob Roach.

Moft’s Snap-on Phone Stand and Wallet is another good kickstand wallet option. You can set it up at three angles: one for scrolling through your phone, one for streaming media, and one for video conferencing. It feels sturdy, and the case isn’t bulky. I wouldn’t put more than two cards in this one, though. I usually use it to carry my license and debit card, while the rest are in my Apple Wallet. —Brenda Stolyar.

Sources indicate that alternatively, Moft sells a trackable version with Apple Find My capabilities. It even comes in versions that can match your iPhone. It isn’t super roomy, but I still like it.

ESR Geo Wallet Stand for $47: Apple’s Find My app lets you track your devices if they’re lost, and ESR’s Geo wallet has it built right into the wallet itself. This is the wallet I’ve been using for the past few weeks, and outside of its Find My capabilities, I love that it strikes a great balance between size and usability. ESR claims it can hold up to three cards, but I’ve been using mine with four—three cards plus my ID—and I can get them all out easily. Although having a wallet with magnetic charging pins is weird—the Find My feature requires a battery that lasts three months—you can turn it off if you don’t care for it (but then, maybe just buy a different wallet). It does kind of suck that you need a proprietary charger to recharge your wallet, though. The magnets adhere well to the back of the phone, and you can pop open the wallet and use it as a kickstand. ESR even includes a strap on the back that works as a phone grip.

Recent findings suggest that otterBox Symmetry Series Cactus Leather MagSafe Wallet for $45: This wallet is nice and simple, thin, lightweight, has a strong hold on my phone case, and offers a dedicated fabric-covered slot at the bottom to push the cards out (I was able to fit three without much trouble). This OtterBox wallet is made from cactus-based leather, which feels nearly as luxurious as real leather. Just know that cactus leather isn’t as eco-friendly as it’s made out to be—these cases are still infused with layers of plastic.

In a recent development, spigen MagSafe Classic LS Wallet for $40: This cool-looking wallet incorporates design inspiration from the classic Macintosh computers. The gray might seem a little bit drab, but any Apple enthusiast will likely enjoy the nod to the computers of yesteryear. It’s otherwise pretty standard fare, with space for up to three cards. I like the thumb notch, which makes it easy to slide your cards out.

It has been revealed that pelican Protector MagSafe Wallet: This MagSafe wallet is simply too bulky. It’s difficult to slip into a pocket, and we don’t think the protective hardshell is worth the trade-off since it can only hold two or three cards.

In a recent development, kate Spade Fresh York Morgan MagSafe Wallet: This wallet looks nice, but the finish starts to degrade with regular use. It also opened on its own once or twice, which left me worried about a card slipping out.

According to recent reports, ohsnap! Snap Grip Wallet: I had high hopes for this one, mainly because of its build quality. The wallet is aluminum, can hold up to eight cards (depending on whether they have raised lettering or not), has MagSafe support, and comes with a grip that doubles as a kickstand. Unfortunately, the grip is made of plastic, and it broke after a short time (it won’t fold properly back into place). The magnetic hold isn’t as strong as other MagSafe wallets, even with a MagSafe-approved case on my phone. None of that is great, especially at this high price.

Apple FineWoven MagSafe Case: Any time this wallet is separated from your iPhone, you’ll get an alert and can track it in Apple’s Find My app. It has a single slot that fits up to three cards, but to remove them, you have to take it off your iPhone and push the cards up through the slot on the back. Unfortunately, Apple’s MagSafe wallets use only the company’s proprietary FineWoven material (made from recycled materials). It’s a commendable effort to reduce reliance on leather production, but several WIRED reviewers have mentioned the material doesn’t hold up well over time.

Journey Loc8 Universal MagSafe Slim Wallet: My cards would slip out of this wallet if I didn’t have it stuffed full, which makes it an obvious “Do Not Recommend” choice when so many other comparable wallets don’t have this problem.

Amazon Relational Database Service (RDS) for PostgreSQL now supports the latest minor versions 18.7, 17.12, 16.16, 15.20, and 14.25. We recommend that you upgrade to the latest minor versions to address Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) in prior versions of PostgreSQL, and to benefit from the bug fixes and improvements added by the PostgreSQL community.

According to recent reports, you can upgrade your databases during scheduled maintenance windows using automatic minor version upgrades. To simplify operations at scale, enable automatic minor version upgrades and use the AWS Organizations Upgrade Rollout Policy to orchestrate multiple upgrades in phases, validating on lower-priority environments before upgrading your most critical ones. You can also use Amazon RDS Blue/Green deployments to minimize downtime for minor version upgrades. For more information, see Upgrading RDS for PostgreSQL DB engine.

According to recent reports, amazon RDS for PostgreSQL makes it simple to set up, operate, and scale PostgreSQL deployments in the cloud. See Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL Pricing for pricing details and regional availability. Create or update a fully managed Amazon RDS database in the Amazon RDS Management Console or by using the AWS Command Line Interface (CLI).

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Amazon ↗ Open Full Page

Amazon Neptune introduces Neptune Graph Sessions, smaller graphs designed for agents that scale to zero and resume automatically

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (294 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon Neptune now supports Neptune Graph Sessions, a compute mode designed for agents that scales memory and CPU automatically and scales to zero when idle.
  • Applications such as GraphRAG assistants, AI agents and per-user analytics improve accuracy when using a graph.
  • When a graph is idle, Graph Sessions scales to zero automatically after 15 minutes, and the graph resumes in seconds when the next query arrives.

Amazon Neptune now supports Neptune Graph Sessions, a compute mode designed for agents that scales memory and CPU automatically and scales to zero when idle. You can give each agent, user or task its own graph without paying for the 16 m-NCU minimum of a provisioned graph. You choose a starting size of 4 s-NCU (sessions Neptune capacity units) or 8 s-NCU of working memory when you create a graph.

Applications such as GraphRAG assistants, AI agents and per-user analytics improve accuracy when using a graph. These use cases often need a separate graph for each conversation or task, and the size of that graph is hard to predict. Each Graph Sessions graph starts at the size you choose and includes memory headroom up to twice that size for the data you load and the queries you run (a 4 s-NCU graph has up to 8 s-NCU of memory, and an 8 s-NCU graph has up to 16 s-NCU), so the starting size does not have to cover your largest graph. You are billed for the memory your graph uses, so a graph that fits in the smaller size is billed at the smaller size.

When a graph is idle, Graph Sessions scales to zero automatically after 15 minutes, and the graph resumes in seconds when the next query arrives. Your graph and its data are kept, so you do not reload data for each session and pay for the running price.

According to recent reports, you can create a Neptune Graph Sessions graph using the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, or AWS SDKs, and query it with openCypher like any other Neptune Analytics graph. For more information, see the Neptune Analytics User Guide and the Amazon Neptune pricing page.

10 Best Office Chairs of 2026—We Tested 70 to Pick Them
